sections.title: History
sections.text: Domaines Ott traces its history to Marcel Ott in the early twentieth century. He acquired Château de Selle in 1912. The name represents a family-founded group of estates and a wider wine portfolio.

sections.title: People and ownership
sections.text: The official website identifies Domaines Ott as part of the Roederer Collection. The group comprises three distinct estates; detailed shareholdings and their chronology are not documented in the sources used here.

sections.title: Vineyards and sites
sections.text: Château de Selle is at Taradeau in Côtes de Provence; Clos Mireille is at coastal La Londe-les-Maures, also in Côtes de Provence; Château Romassan is near Le Castellet in Bandol. Étoile combines fruit from the three estates and is classified Vin de France.

sections.title: Portfolio
sections.text: The portfolio includes Château de Selle, Clos Mireille and Château Romassan estate wines, the cross-estate Étoile cuvée and the BY.OTT range. Individual wine profiles in this first edition cover a selection of the portfolio.

sections.title: History
sections.text: Château de Selle, at Taradeau near Draguignan, was the first estate purchased by Marcel Ott, in 1912. It is one of the three Domaines Ott estates and produces Côtes de Provence wines.

sections.title: People and ownership
sections.text: An estate within Domaines Ott, whose official website identifies an affiliation with the Roederer Collection. The detailed legal ownership chronology of the estate is not documented in this profile.

sections.title: Vineyards and sites
sections.text: The estate describes approximately 93 hectares of planted vines around Taradeau, with gypsum, red clay, sandstone, gravel and stones. These figures and soils concern Château de Selle.

sections.title: Portfolio
sections.text: Château de Selle Rosé is a Côtes de Provence AOC wine. The estate catalogue also includes a red wine; a complete vintage-by-vintage portfolio is outside this first edition.

sections.title: History
sections.text: Raymond-Étienne Amiel acquired the property in 1816. Charles Dupuy acquired it in 1907, and successive Dupuy generations developed its reputation for vins doux naturels. Olivier Decelle began a period of renewal in 1999, developing dry wines alongside fortified Maury.

sections.title: People and ownership
sections.text: The estate chronology records Raymond-Étienne Amiel from 1816, the Charles and Jean Dupuy family era from 1907 to 1997, and Olivier Decelle’s transformation from 1999. These historical roles do not establish current shareholding percentages.

sections.title: Vineyards and sites
sections.text: Mas Amiel lies in the Agly valley at Maury, Roussillon. The estate page describes about 95 parcels and 100 hectares of vineyards, including old Grenache and Carignan on schist and calcareous schist. A historical 1999 account gives 155 planted hectares within a 226-hectare property; the figures refer to different dates and definitions. The estate reports organic certification in 2017 and biodynamic certification by 2020.

sections.title: Portfolio
sections.text: The fortified portfolio includes Vintage Rouge, Vintage Réserve, Vintage Charles Dupuy, Vintage Blanc, aged oxidative blends and vintage-dated Maury. The Trésors du Temps selection includes 20, 30, 40 and 50 Ans d’Âge. Dry wines include Maury Sec and Côtes du Roussillon. Availability and individual cuvée specifications depend on the release.

producers.name: Clos Cibonne
producers.regionLinkScope: geographic_context; exact wine origin is separate
producers.intro: Clos Cibonne is a Roux family estate at Le Pradet in Provence. André Roux (1905–1989) championed Tibouren and helped establish the estate’s Côtes de Provence Cru Classé standing. His daughter Jacqueline and son-in-law Émile ran the estate from 1989 to 2003; later family accounts document Brigitte, Claude, Olivier and Caroline.

sections.title: History
sections.text: Clos Cibonne is a Roux family estate at Le Pradet in Provence. André Roux (1905–1989) championed Tibouren and helped establish the estate’s Côtes de Provence Cru Classé standing. His daughter Jacqueline and son-in-law Émile ran the estate from 1989 to 2003; later family accounts document Brigitte, Claude, Olivier and Caroline.

sections.title: People and ownership
sections.text: The estate describes Olivier joining in 2012 to lead viticulture and winemaking, Brigitte in sales and administration, Claude in commercial development, and Caroline contributing to communications. These are source-era responsibilities; current beneficial shareholdings are not documented here.

sections.title: Vineyards and sites
sections.text: The coastal Le Pradet estate is a Tibouren specialist and one of Provence’s historical Cru Classé estates. Tradition combines Tibouren and Grenache. Cuvée des Vignettes draws on vines dating from the mid-1950s. The Prestige cuvées Caroline and Olivier use 300-litre barrels.

sections.title: Portfolio
sections.text: The estate catalogue includes Tradition, Tentations, Cuvée des Vignettes and the Prestige wines Caroline Rosé and Olivier Rouge. Historical Cuvée Spéciale Tibouren naming and vintage-specific releases require their corresponding labels and technical sheets.

producers.name: Domaine Jules Desjourneys
producers.regionLinkScope: geographic_context; exact wine origin is separate
producers.intro: Jules Desjourneys began wine production in 2007 with Fleurie and Moulin-à-Vent. The source chronology dates Chénas Le Jugement Dernier and later Chassignol-related releases from 2012. The portfolio subsequently extended into Mâconnais whites. The literary account of “Jules” on the website is brand storytelling, not evidence of a historical founder of that name.

sections.title: History
sections.text: Jules Desjourneys began wine production in 2007 with Fleurie and Moulin-à-Vent. The source chronology dates Chénas Le Jugement Dernier and later Chassignol-related releases from 2012. The portfolio subsequently extended into Mâconnais whites. The literary account of “Jules” on the website is brand storytelling, not evidence of a historical founder of that name.

sections.title: People and ownership
sections.text: The official legal notice names SARL Jules Desjourneys, gives an address at La Chapelle-de-Guinchay, and identifies Fabien Duperray as publication manager. It does not establish complete corporate shareholdings or vineyard land titles.

sections.title: Vineyards and sites
sections.text: Origins include Fleurie sites Les Moriers and Chapelle des Bois, Moulin-à-Vent sites Chassignol and Aux Michelons, Chénas Le Jugement Dernier, and Pouilly-Fuissé in the Mâconnais. Chassignol is described as old vines on quartz-rich granite. Each wine retains its own geographical origin.

sections.title: Portfolio
sections.text: Documented cuvées include Moulin-à-Vent Chassignol and Aux Michelons, Fleurie Les Moriers and La Chapelle des Bois, Chénas Le Jugement Dernier, and Pouilly-Fuissé Les Vignes Blanches. Historical “Les Michelons” naming and references to Les Ménétrières require vintage-specific labels for precise comparison. The current red-wine portfolio is broader than this selection.

Antoine Abbatucci established a collection of traditional Corsican grape varieties; Jean-Charles developed biodynamic farming and heritage-variety research. The Collection range, celebrating historical family figures, began in 2006.

sections.title: History
sections.text: The family estate lies at Casalabriva in the Taravo valley of southern Corsica. Antoine Abbatucci established a collection of traditional Corsican grape varieties; Jean-Charles developed biodynamic farming and heritage-variety research. The Collection range, celebrating historical family figures, began in 2006.

sections.title: People and ownership
sections.text: The estate website names Jean-Charles and his daughter Faustine Abbatucci as proprietor-vignerons. Its 2026 legal notice identifies EARL Domaine Comte Abbatucci. Detailed beneficial shareholdings are not given.

sections.title: Vineyards and sites
sections.text: The estate describes 21 hectares of vines on decomposed granitic sands near 150 metres altitude in the Taravo valley. Its ampelographic collection conserves a range of native grapes; the estate area is not an individual cuvée’s vineyard area.

sections.title: Viticulture
sections.text: Biodynamic cultivation and conservation of Corsican grapes are central to the estate’s stated approach. The website’s reference to 18 old or native varieties concerns the conservatory, not the blend of every wine.

sections.title: Vinification
sections.text: Methods vary by range. Faustine whites and rosés largely use stainless steel; the red uses a longer maceration. Collection whites combine demi-muids and stainless steel. Parcellaires wines may use foudres, demi-muids or tanks. Wine-specific technical sheets define the relevant process.

sections.title: Portfolio
sections.text: The portfolio includes Faustine Blanc, Rouge and Rosé; the Parcellaires wines Alte Rosso Blanc, Monte Bianco Rouge and Valle di Nero Rosé; and Collection wines Ministre Impérial Rouge, Diplomate d’Empire Blanc and Général de la Révolution Blanc. The current Ministre Impérial technical sheet specifies Vin de France. Historical Faustine Vieilles Vignes Rosé naming requires a corresponding release label. Other estate ranges include Empire Sparkling, Dolce Rosso and the Insolites Valle di Mare and Monte Mare.

sections.title: History
sections.text: Domaine Gauby is a family property centred on Calce in Roussillon, associated with terroir-focused wines and organic, biodynamic and regenerative farming. Distributor and regional accounts describe Gérard Gauby’s development of the estate and Lionel Gauby’s subsequent role in vinification.

sections.title: People and ownership
sections.text: Gérard Gauby established and expanded the domaine; distributor accounts identify Lionel with later winemaking and estate stewardship. Family roles, company representatives and land ownership are distinct matters; detailed current shareholdings are not established here.

sections.title: Vineyards and sites
sections.text: Distributor and regional sources describe an approximately 85-hectare ecosystem: around 45 hectares of vines and 40 hectares of grassland, woodland and garrigue. Sites lie near 150–200 metres altitude, with limestone, marl and schist under Mediterranean influence. Some vines exceed a century in age. Areas and vine ages are source-specific.

sections.title: Viticulture
sections.text: Distributors describe organic and biodynamic cultivation with preparations made at the estate. These farming descriptions do not, by themselves, document a current certification.

sections.title: Vinification
sections.text: Whole-bunch handling, carbonic maceration and maturation vary by wine and period. The 2023 La Muntada description specifies 70% Grenache and 30% Carignan, with 14 months in foudre and concrete. That release is IGP Côtes Catalanes; older Côtes du Roussillon Villages descriptions belong to their respective vintages.

sections.title: Portfolio
sections.text: The distributor’s 2026 list includes Les Calcinaires Blanc and Rouge, Vieilles Vignes Blanc and Rouge, La Muntada Rouge, Coume Gineste Blanc and La Jasse, under IGP Côtes Catalanes. Historical references also include La Roque. Colour and vintage distinguish wines that share a cuvée name.

producers.name: Domaine Jean Foillard
producers.regionLinkScope: geographic_context; exact wine origin is separate
producers.intro: Jean and Agnès Foillard took over Jean’s father’s property in 1980. Jean became associated with the Beaujolais low-intervention movement influenced by Jules Chauvet and the group often called the “Gang of Four”: Lapierre, Thévenet, Breton and Foillard. This history is documented by importer Kermit Lynch.

sections.title: History
sections.text: Jean and Agnès Foillard took over Jean’s father’s property in 1980. Jean became associated with the Beaujolais low-intervention movement influenced by Jules Chauvet and the group often called the “Gang of Four”: Lapierre, Thévenet, Breton and Foillard. This history is documented by importer Kermit Lynch.

sections.title: People and ownership
sections.text: Importer sources identify Jean and Agnès with the 1980 takeover. Alex Foillard also appears as an associated grower, with a distinct portfolio; current legal shareholding percentages are not documented in this profile.

sections.title: Vineyards and sites
sections.text: The importer describes close to 14 hectares at the time of publication, including Morgon Côte du Py, Corcelette, Les Charmes and Fleurie. Côte du Py descriptions refer to schist, granite and manganese; Corcelette is lighter and sandy. Cuvée 3.14 draws on very old Gamay, described as around a century old. Portfolio-wide vineyard totals are not individual cuvée areas.

sections.title: Viticulture
sections.text: The importer reports certified organic farming, hand sorting, restrained sulphur use and unfiltered bottling. These descriptions are tied to the importer’s publication, rather than a separately examined current certificate.

sections.title: Vinification
sections.text: For several Morgon cuvées, the importer describes traditional whole-bunch, semi-carbonic fermentation over three to four weeks and six to nine months in used Burgundy barrels. Corcelette may also use a 30-hectolitre foudre. Timing and vessels may vary by vintage.

sections.title: Portfolio
sections.text: The Morgon selection includes Côte du Py, Corcelette, Cuvée 3.14 and Les Charmes, also encountered as Eponym’. The importer additionally lists Beaujolais-Villages and Fleurie. Cuvée 3.14 is a selected very-old-vine expression whose release is vintage-dependent.

sections.title: History
sections.text: Hervé and Claudine Bizeul established Domaine du Clos des Fées at Vingrau in Roussillon in the late 1990s. Estate and importer accounts describe a portfolio assembled from small parcels across several Roussillon terroirs.

sections.title: People and ownership
sections.text: Hervé Bizeul is identified as founder and vigneron, with Claudine Bizeul in the estate’s historical account. A current corporate shareholding breakdown is not documented in the sources used here.

sections.title: Vineyards and sites
sections.text: The estate works a mosaic of limestone-clay, marl and schist sites around Vingrau, exposed to the Tramontane. A 2025 importer catalogue describes approximately 30 hectares across several terroirs and more than 100 plots. La Petite Sibérie is a particular old-vine, Grenache-dominant, wind-exposed parcel; these estate-wide figures are not its area.

sections.title: Portfolio
sections.text: Principal names include Le Clos des Fées, Vieilles Vignes, Les Sorcières, La Petite Sibérie and De battre mon cœur s’est arrêté. Vieilles Vignes and Les Sorcières occur in both red and white forms. The 2023 Post Scriptum release has a distinct identity from standard La Petite Sibérie. Appellation, colour and technical details require the corresponding wine and vintage.

producers.name: Domaine Marcel Lapierre
producers.regionLinkScope: geographic_context; exact wine origin is separate
producers.intro: The family history in Villié-Morgon begins with Michel Lapierre in 1909. His son Camille developed bottling; Marcel took over in 1973 and, influenced by Jules Chauvet, began pursuing vinification without added sulphur in 1981. Marcel died in October 2010. Mathieu joined in 2004 and assumed management in 2010; his sister Camille joined in 2013. The name “M & C Lapierre” refers to the same family estate.

sections.title: History
sections.text: The family history in Villié-Morgon begins with Michel Lapierre in 1909. His son Camille developed bottling; Marcel took over in 1973 and, influenced by Jules Chauvet, began pursuing vinification without added sulphur in 1981. Marcel died in October 2010. Mathieu joined in 2004 and assumed management in 2010; his sister Camille joined in 2013. The name “M & C Lapierre” refers to the same family estate.

sections.title: People and ownership
sections.text: The family account includes Marcel, Mathieu, Camille, Anne and Marie. Mathieu’s management and winemaking role dates from 2010; Camille joined in 2013. Marie is associated with historical viticulture and sales responsibilities. Detailed current beneficial shareholdings are not stated.

sections.title: Vineyards and sites
sections.text: The estate’s 2026 website reports approximately 20 hectares of Gamay noir à jus blanc, predominantly in Morgon with some Beaujolais sites. Cuvée Camille comes from a southwest-facing Côte du Py site on shallow granitic bedrock; an older technical sheet gives one hectare. These figures have different geographical and chronological scopes.

sections.title: Viticulture
sections.text: The estate reports organic certification since 2004 and a farming approach developed from around 1981.

sections.title: Vinification
sections.text: Hand harvesting and sorting precede semi-carbonic Beaujolais maceration with indigenous yeast. Sulphur additions during vinification are limited or absent, while bottling practice varies by wine and batch. Cuvée Camille receives a longer maceration in a wooden truncated-conical vat; exact timing is vintage-dependent.

sections.title: Portfolio
sections.text: Morgon and Cuvée Camille are part of a wider portfolio that includes Cuvée Marcel Lapierre, Raisins Gaulois, Beaujolais and Bourgogne Pinot Noir. Cuvée Camille has historical Roche du Py and Côte du Py references; it is distinct from Cuvée Marcel Lapierre.

producers.name: Domaine Jean-Marc Burgaud
producers.regionLinkScope: geographic_context; exact wine origin is separate
producers.intro: Jean-Marc Burgaud founded the Villié-Morgon estate in 1989. Its 2026 website reports 17.5 hectares in Beaujolais: 12.5 in Morgon and five in Lantignié. Morgon expressions include Côte du Py, Javernières, La Roche, James, Ruyère and Chollet.

sections.title: History
sections.text: Jean-Marc Burgaud founded the Villié-Morgon estate in 1989. Its 2026 website reports 17.5 hectares in Beaujolais: 12.5 in Morgon and five in Lantignié. Morgon expressions include Côte du Py, Javernières, La Roche, James, Ruyère and Chollet.

sections.title: People and ownership
sections.text: Jean-Marc Burgaud is the founder and winemaker. The sources used here do not establish a detailed current shareholding or succession structure.

sections.title: Vineyards and sites
sections.text: Côte du Py is described as a south-facing hill of blue schist rich in iron oxides, alongside the estate’s separate granite and clay sites. A dated commercial account refers to six hectares at Côte du Py; the estate’s 12.5 hectares in Morgon represent a broader area.

sections.title: Viticulture
sections.text: An organic certification is not established by the sources used in this first edition.

sections.title: Vinification
sections.text: Estate and importer sources describe whole-cluster Gamay maceration. A Côte du Py importer profile gives seven to twelve days; an older technical sheet gives twelve to fourteen. These are source-specific descriptions, rather than a fixed protocol for every vintage.

sections.title: Portfolio
sections.text: The estate lists Lantignié whites and reds alongside Morgon Chollet, Ruyère, La Roche, Côte du Py, Javernières and James. This first edition includes an individual Côte du Py profile.
